```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(docdesigner)
tokens <- designer_tokens()
```

A docdesigner style is one file, `format.yml`, that lists design decisions
as tokens: `color.accent`, `typography.base_size`, `headings.h1.scale`, and
so on. The engine turns those tokens into LaTeX. You never write LaTeX, and a
style cannot break a document: every token is checked against a schema with
fixed types, bounds and named steps.

This guide assumes you design a style with an AI assistant. You decide what
the style is for and judge every page. The assistant writes the file, checks
it and renders it. The split plays to each side: an assistant writes valid
tokens quickly once it has the vocabulary, and a person sees at a glance
whether a page works.

The guide covers the workflow, the context to give the assistant, the rules
for setting tokens, the principles that separate a good style from a merely
valid one, and markup styles for drafts. It closes with the full token
reference. Everything after the workflow is background for both of you: for
you, to judge the result; for the assistant, to produce it.

# The workflow

1. **Write a context folder** with `designer_ai_context()`. It gathers the
   files that make an assistant accurate; the next section lists them.
2. **Give the folder to the assistant**, `AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md` first.
3. **Say what the style is for**: the kind of document, who reads it and
   how, and anything it should resemble. Pictures of pages you admire do
   more than adjectives.
4. **The assistant drafts.** It copies the nearest shipped style, changes
   only the tokens that differ, writes a reason beside each, then validates
   and renders with the folder's `check-style.R`.
5. **You look at the pages** and say what is wrong. Repeat 4 and 5.
6. **Read the finished `format.yml`.** Every token should carry a reason
   you agree with. Then share it, as a folder or inside a set.

```r
# 1. The context folder, built around the style you will start from.
#    Name two or three other styles to show the assistant the range.
designer_ai_context("my-context", from = "policy", examples = c("economist", "minimal"))
```

A first message to the assistant can be as short as this:

> Read `AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md` and the files beside it. I want a style for
> two-page briefs on housing policy, read by city officials on paper and on
> screen. It should feel authoritative but not academic. I've attached three
> pages from briefs I like. Start from `policy`.

The assistant's loop runs four commands. You can run them yourself at any
point:

```r
# Copy the nearest shipped style. complete = FALSE copies only the tokens
# that style declares, so the draft stays short and every line is a choice.
designer_new_style("my-brief", from = "policy", path = ".", complete = FALSE)

# Errors must be fixed. Warnings flag risky combinations.
designer_validate_style("my-brief")

# Render any document with the draft by pointing at its folder.
rmarkdown::render("paper.Rmd", output_format = docdesigner::pdf(style = "my-brief"))
```

```sh
# Or all three steps, plus an image of every page, in one:
Rscript my-context/check-style.R my-brief
```

Inside a document's YAML header the style is named the same way:

```yaml
output:
  docdesigner::pdf:
    style: "path/to/my-brief"
    title_layout: page        # optional: override the style's title.layout
```

The folder's `specimen.md` shows every element a style sets in a few pages.
Before you finish, also render a document that looks like your real work:
figures, tables of different shapes, a long title, an abstract, footnotes, a
block quote and references. `examples/gallery-document.Rmd` in the source
repository carries all of these.

# What to give the assistant

An assistant left to its memory writes YAML that resembles a style but names
tokens and values docdesigner does not have. These files fix that. All of
them except the last two come from `designer_ai_context()`, generated from
the installed package, so they match the version you render with. Write the
folder again after updating docdesigner.

| File | Also available as | What it gives the assistant |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md` | | How to work: what to ask you first, the loop, the validator's cross-token rules, and the mistakes assistants make most. Load it first. |
| `brief.md` | `designer_design_brief()` | The hard constraints: colour roles, fonts, named steps, the type scale, title layouts, markup styles. |
| `tokens.csv` | `designer_tokens()` | Every key that exists, with its allowed values, default and status. The commonest failure is an invented key. |
| `examples/*.yml` | `designer_new_style()` | Shipped styles with their authors' comments. An assistant imitates what it sees, so show it reasoned files. |
| `specimen.md` | | A test document with every element a style sets. |
| `check-style.R` | | The loop as one script: validate, render, write each page as a PNG. Needs the pdftools package for the images. |
| This article | [the website](https://jncohen.github.io/docdesigner/articles/creating-styles.html) | What makes a style good, not just valid. The brief says what is allowed; this says what works. |
| Your model pages | | Screenshots or PDF pages of what the style should resemble. The single most useful input when imitating a publication. |

How you hand these over depends on the assistant.

- **An assistant that runs code and reads images**, such as a coding
  assistant opened on the folder, runs `check-style.R` itself and looks at
  the pages before showing them to you. Your part is to judge.
- **A chat assistant without tools** gets the files as attachments and
  writes `format.yml`. You run the script, paste back the validator's
  output, and attach the page images. It is slower, and it works.

Either way, hold the assistant to the page. It will describe a draft as
clean, balanced or readable; only a render shows whether it is (see *Only
the page is evidence*, below). Ask for the images, and look at every one.

To imitate a design made in a visual tool rather than describe it, export
the design as one standalone HTML page and translate it with
`designer_import_html()`. The brief's last section says what the import
reads and what it leaves to you.

# Setting tokens

## The format

Keys are flat and dotted, one per line. Comments are encouraged; record
*why* a value was chosen, not what it is.

```yaml
id: my-brief                 # required; lowercase letters, digits, hyphens
label: "My Brief"            # required; how the style is listed
description: >               # recommended; what it is for and what it imitates
  A two-page policy brief with a sans kicker and a tinted callout.
inherits: policy             # optional; see below

color.accent: "#0B5E55"
typography.base_size: 10.5pt
title.layout: page
callout.style: boxed
```

Each key appears once. To change a value the scaffold already declares, edit
that line; adding the same key again further down is a YAML error.

## Six rules

1. **Declare only what differs.** Every token has a default. A style that
   restates defaults freezes them: when the engine's default improves, your
   style will not follow.
2. **Hex colours live only under `color.*`.** Everywhere else a token names a
   colour *role*: `accent`, `accent2`, `text`, `muted`, `rule`, `background`,
   `code_bg` or `knockout`. Change the palette in one place and every element
   that uses a role follows. Quote hex values (`"#0B5E55"`); unquoted, YAML can
   read some of them as numbers.
3. **Lengths are named steps, not dimensions.** `quote.indent: md`, not
   `quote.indent: 1em`. The steps are fixed scales (space, indent, rule
   weight, gutter, margin, width), so styles stay consistent with one another
   and cannot produce invalid LaTeX. Margins are the exception: `page.margins.*`
   take inches, because a page design needs asymmetric margins.
4. **Sizes are multiples.** Heading, title, caption and table sizes are set
   relative to `typography.base_size`, so changing the body size rescales the
   whole hierarchy.
5. **Use `inherits` for families of styles.** `inherits: policy` starts from
   policy's declared tokens and applies yours on top. Chains resolve from the
   root, and a cycle or missing parent is an error.
6. **Check a token's status before relying on it.** `impl` tokens render.
   `new` tokens validate and are ignored until the engine implements them;
   `designer_validate_style()` lists them. `deprecated` tokens still work and
   name their replacement.

The validator also applies cross-token rules:

```{r rules, echo = FALSE}
rules <- yaml::read_yaml(system.file("engine", "schema.yml", package = "docdesigner"))$rules
knitr::kable(data.frame(Rule = vapply(rules, `[[`, "", "id"),
                        Meaning = vapply(rules, `[[`, "", "doc")),
             format = "pipe")
```

## Structure versus look

Two kinds of decision go into a page, and docdesigner keeps them apart.

**Structure** is what goes where. `title.layout` is the main structural
token: `header` sets the title block at the head of the first page, and `page`
gives the title and abstract a page of their own. `page.columns` (one or two)
is the other. Because structure varies by occasion as much as by style, the
title layout can also be chosen per document with
`pdf(title_layout = "page")`.

**Look** is everything else: faces, sizes, colours, rules, spacing, and how
each element (title, abstract, headings, quotes, callouts, tables, captions,
running heads) is treated. Look tokens apply in every layout. A centred
small-caps title with a short rule is centred, small-caps and ruled whether it
opens page 1 or stands on a title page.

Design the look once and check it in both layouts.

## Block elements

Three elements set text apart from the body, and a style should make them
distinguishable at a glance.

| Element | Written as | Tokens | Use it for |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Block quote | `> text` | `quote.*` | Someone else's words |
| Callout | `::: {.callout title="..."}` | `callout.*` | The author's own key point |
| Abstract | `abstract:` in the YAML header | `title.abstract.*` | The summary |

`callout.style` takes `filled` (a tinted panel), `ruled` (a bar at the left),
`boxed` (a border round a tint) or `plain` (indented text under a title). If
the style's quotes already carry a left bar, do not give callouts one too:
readers will take the two for the same thing. The shipped styles show the
pattern. atlantic, economist, modern and nature rule their quotes and fill
their callouts; methods, which boxes its abstract, boxes its callouts to
match.

# Principles of good style

A style passes validation the moment its keys and values are legal. These
principles decide whether it is any good. Each comes with the check that tells
you whether you have met it.

## Measure: 45 to 75 characters per line

Line length governs reading comfort more than any other single choice. Below
about 45 characters the eye jumps lines too often; above about 75 it loses
its place on the return sweep. Aim for 60 to 72 in a single column and 40 to
55 in each of two.

Estimate it before you render. For a typical book serif, a line holds about

$$\text{characters} \approx \frac{\text{text width in points}}{0.47 \times \text{body size in points}}$$

An 8.5-inch page with 1.85-inch side margins leaves 4.8 inches (346 pt); at
10.5 pt that is about 70 characters. Then count
a few full lines on the rendered page.

Wide margins look generous on screen and wasteful in print. If a comfortable
measure leaves the margins too wide, raise the body size by half a point, or
use two columns, before you shrink the margins.

## Leading: open enough to track, tight enough to hold

`typography.line_height` multiplies LaTeX's own leading, which is already
about 1.2 times the type size. Values from 1.1 to 1.25 suit most text faces.
Open the leading as the measure lengthens; tighten it for short lines and
large type. Display text (titles, headings, captions, tables, footnotes) keeps
its own spacing whatever this token says.

## Hierarchy: few signals, used consistently

A reader should be able to tell a section from a subsection without reading
the words. Use the fewest signals that achieve it: size, weight, case, colour,
rules, numbering. Two or three distinct heading levels are enough for almost
any paper.

- Keep the size steps modest. `h1` at 1.3 to 1.5 times the body, `h2` at 1.1
  to 1.2, `h3` at the body size. Large jumps look like a poster.
- Change one signal per level where possible. If `h2` is bold, `h3` can be
  bold italic or small capitals at the same size.
- Do not repeat a signal for two different jobs. If the accent colour marks
  headings, a link in the same colour reads as a heading fragment.

## Colour: one accent, used sparingly

Most good document designs use near-black text, one grey for secondary
material, and a single accent. The accent carries meaning only while it is
rare: put it on the title rule, the section numbers or headings, links, and
callouts, and nowhere else. A second accent (`color.accent2`) is for data
graphics that need two series, not for decoration.

Check contrast. Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against
the page (WCAG AA), and so does any coloured text a reader must read, such as
captions in `muted` or links in `accent`. A light grey that looks refined on a
screen often fails on paper.

```{r contrast}
contrast <- function(fg, bg = "#FFFFFF") {
  lum <- function(hex) {
    c <- grDevices::col2rgb(hex)[, 1] / 255
    c <- ifelse(c <= 0.03928, c / 12.92, ((c + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4)
    sum(c(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722) * c)
  }
  l <- sort(c(lum(fg), lum(bg)), decreasing = TRUE)
  round((l[1] + 0.05) / (l[2] + 0.05), 1)
}
pal <- designer_style("modern")$color
sapply(pal[c("text", "accent", "muted")], contrast)
```

## Paragraphs: indent or space, never both

Separate paragraphs with a first-line indent (`paragraph.indent`) or with
vertical space (`paragraph.spacing`), not both. Indents suit continuous
argument and long reading; space suits reports that a reader scans. The
validator warns if you set both.

## Tables: let the data carry the structure

Horizontal rules at the top, under the header and at the bottom
(`table.style: booktabs`) suit nearly every research table. Vertical rules and
full grids add noise without helping the eye along a row. Set tables slightly
smaller than the body (`table.size` about 0.9) and keep their leading close
(`table.row_stretch` 1.1 to 1.25). Right-align numbers; that is the author's
job (in `knitr::kable`, `align = "lrr"`), not the style's.

## Faces: open, legible, and few

Use one family for text and at most one more for contrast, typically a sans
for labels, kickers and table headers (`typography.label`). Never name a
proprietary face: a style that imitates a publication uses an open substitute
with similar proportions and records the original in `description`. The
bundled families are Source Serif 4, EB Garamond, XITS and Fira Code; a style
can ship others under `fonts.<Family>.<face>`.

## Fit the occasion

A style is for a kind of document read by a kind of reader. A journal
manuscript under review wants plain structure, a header title, wide spacing
(`pdf(doublespace = TRUE)`) and no ornament. A policy brief wants a kicker, a
strong title, a callout for the finding, and a page a busy reader can scan. A
long essay wants a book face, indented paragraphs, and quiet headings. Decide
who reads the document and how, then choose.

## Only the page is evidence

A token can be correct in `format.yml`, correct in the resolved spec, and
still wrong on the page. Look at every page of a realistic render, in both
title layouts, before you share a style. In particular check:

- a two-line title, and a long author line;
- a table wider than half the measure, in a two-column style;
- the last page, which often carries only a few references;
- the first page of the body when `title.layout` is `page`.

# Markup styles

Most styles dress a finished document for a reader. A markup style dresses a
draft for its author: it is printed to be read slowly and written on, and
every mark made on the page has to lead back to a spot in the source. The
shipped `review` style is the example, and the right starting point:

```r
designer_ai_context("my-context", from = "review")
```

The `markup.*` tokens make a style a markup style. Each is off by default, so
no publication style shows them.

```{r markup-tokens, echo = FALSE}
mk <- tokens[grepl("^markup[.]", tokens$key), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(Token = paste0("`", mk$key, "`"),
                        Default = ifelse(is.na(mk$default), "", mk$default),
                        Effect = gsub("|", "\\|", mk$doc, fixed = TRUE)),
             format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE)
```

A markup style answers to different rules from a publication style.

- **One column.** Line numbers, paragraph numbers, tags and changebars live in
  the margins. The validator warns when a markup style sets two columns.
- **A wide outer margin.** It is where the reader writes. Any `markup.*`
  token lifts the 1.25in margin cap, and `page.margins.outer` may go to 3.5in;
  `review` uses 3in. One-sided pages (`page.twoside: false`) keep it on the
  right of every page.
- **Nothing floats.** With `markup.floats: false` a table or figure stays
  beside the text that discusses it, so a note about one finds the other.
- **Stable lines.** A short measure, open leading, ragged right and no
  hyphenation keep each line break, and so each line number, the same from
  one printout to the next.
- **The tags belong to the engine.** `[[V]]`, `[[C]]`, `[[TODO]]` and the rest
  are fixed; the README lists them. A style switches them on with
  `markup.flags` and colours them with `markup.flag_color`, but cannot add or
  rename one.

A writer can turn one feature off for one printout without a second style:
`pdf(style = "review", markup = list(line_numbers = 0))`.

When you check the page, check the marks as well as the text: two tags on
one line, a tag under a flagged heading, a changebar beside a table, and line
numbers on a page that opens with a figure.

# Sharing a style

The simplest way to share a style is the folder: anyone can render with
`pdf(style = "path/to/folder")`. To ship several styles together, put them in
a set: a folder holding `set.yml` and `styles/<id>/format.yml` for each style.
Fonts a style needs go in `styles/<id>/assets/fonts/` or the set's own
`assets/fonts/`.

```yaml
# set.yml
id: my-house
title: "My house styles"
version: 1.0.0
format_version: 2
styles: [my-brief, my-paper]
```

`designer_install_set()` installs a set from a GitHub repository, and
`designer_update_sets()` refreshes installed sets. A style in an installed
set with the same id as a core style takes precedence, with a warning.

# Token reference

Every token the engine knows, generated from the schema when this page was
built. **Allowed** gives the legal values: a list of names, a numeric range,
a colour role, or a hex colour. **Status** says whether the engine renders it
today.

```{r reference, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
tokens$group <- sub("\\..*$", "", tokens$key)
tokens$group[tokens$key %in% c("id", "label", "description", "inherits")] <- "identity"
order <- c("identity", "page", "typography", "color", "headings", "title",
           "paragraph", "figure", "table", "code", "quote", "callout",
           "footnotes", "header_footer", "links", "citations")
order <- c(order, setdiff(unique(tokens$group), order))
for (g in order) {
  t <- tokens[tokens$group == g, ]
  if (!nrow(t)) next
  cat("\n## `", g, "`\n\n", sep = "")
  tab <- data.frame(
    Token = paste0("`", t$key, "`"),
    Allowed = gsub("|", "\\|", t$allowed, fixed = TRUE),
    Default = ifelse(is.na(t$default), "", t$default),
    Status = t$status,
    Notes = gsub("|", "\\|", t$doc, fixed = TRUE))
  print(knitr::kable(tab, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE))
  cat("\n")
}
```
